title: Skyroot's Pawan Chandana Named to TIME100 Next 2026 After Vikram-1 Orbital Triumph
excerpt: The Skyroot Aerospace co-founder and CEO joins TIME's annual list of 100 emerging global leaders, months after his company's Vikram-1 became the first Indian private rocket to reach orbit.
body:
• Pawan Kumar Chandana, co-founder and CEO of Skyroot Aerospace, has been named to TIME's TIME100 Next 2026 list of 100 emerging leaders, in the business, technology and AI category.
  • The honour follows Skyroot's July 2026 orbital launch of Vikram-1, which made the Hyderabad startup the first Indian private company to place a rocket into orbit.
  • Chandana, 35, is an IIT Kharagpur alumnus who spent six years as an ISRO scientist before co-founding Skyroot in 2018; the company became India's first space-sector unicorn earlier this year at a valuation of about $1.1 billion.
  • TIME will convene the 2026 TIME100 Next honourees at its sixth annual celebration in New York City on October 29.

Pawan Kumar Chandana, the Hyderabad-born engineer who gave up an ISRO scientist's career to build a private rocket company, has been named to TIME's TIME100 Next 2026 list — the magazine's annual selection of 100 emerging leaders shaping the future across fields.

Chandana, 35, the co-founder and chief executive of Skyroot Aerospace, appears among the business, technology and AI leaders on this year's list, which TIME revealed this week. Skyroot announced the recognition on October 1, describing its chief executive as one of the world's most influential rising stars.

Context & Background

Chandana's path to orbit ran through some of India's most demanding technical institutions. Born in Hyderabad in 1991, he joined the Indian Institute of Technology Kharagpur in 2007 and completed a dual B.Tech-M.Tech programme in mechanical engineering in 2012. He joined the Indian Space Research Organisation straight out of college, working nearly six years as a scientist at the Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre in Thiruvananthapuram on the GSLV Mk-III launch vehicle, its S200 solid rocket booster, and the Small Satellite Launch Vehicle programme.

https://x.com/livemint/status/2106075075405586655

In June 2018, he left ISRO with fellow ex-ISRO engineer Naga Bharath Daka to found Skyroot Aerospace in Hyderabad, betting that India's private sector could build and launch rockets. The gamble paid off in stages: Vikram-S became India's first privately developed rocket to reach space in November 2022, and in July 2026 the company's Vikram-1 successfully reached orbit — the first time an Indian private company placed a rocket into orbit. Earlier this year, Skyroot became India's first space-sector unicorn with a valuation of roughly $1.1 billion.

"It feels quite satisfying, but of course, this is only the very beginning of our journey. We have done only one launch, and we want to do more and more launches."

— Pawan Kumar Chandana, Co-Founder & CEO, Skyroot Aerospace

Impact & Analysis

The TIME100 Next nod is a marker of how far India's commercial space sector has travelled in less than a decade. When Chandana left ISRO in 2018, India's space programme had no private launch company and an uncertain regulatory framework for one. Today, Skyroot anchors an ecosystem the company says spans more than 400 suppliers, with carbon-composite manufacturing being developed in-house and a young engineering team that Chandana has held up as proof of what a new generation of Indian engineers can build at home.

The listing also reflects the economics now attached to the sector: Skyroot's unicorn valuation and the July orbital success have moved the company from a national curiosity to a player in the global small-satellite launch market, where it competes for commercial customers on cost and cadence.

Diaspora Angle

Chandana is one of several Indians and Indian-origin names on this year's TIME100 Next, joining figures such as 15-year-old cricketer Vaibhav Sooryavanshi — the youngest person on the 2026 list — and SpaceX engineer-turned-astronaut Anna Menon among the science and space innovators. For the diaspora, the through-line is talent mobility: Chandana chose to stay and build in India rather than take the campus-placement route abroad, and his company now courts global customers and investors from Hyderabad. India's private space push is increasingly a destination, not just a departure lounge, for aerospace talent.

What's Next

Chandana has said sustainable success depends on launch cadence, not a single mission: more Vikram-1 flights, a stronger domestic supply chain, and — eventually — opportunities from India's military-space requirements. Skyroot is positioning for repeat commercial launches from Indian soil. The next milestone investors and ISRO watchers will track is whether the company can turn one orbital success into a reliable, recurring launch business.
